Chapter Two: The Three Pillars—Giving, Saving, and Spending with Purpose.
Let’s dive into something that sits right at the heart of handling money well. Picture this: three simple, powerful actions—giving, saving, and spending. They’re like the legs of a sturdy stool, and when you balance all three, your financial life just feels more steady.
Each one has its own unique role, and when you weave them together, you get a life that’s not just about numbers, but about meaning and balance.
So, let’s start with giving. Think of giving as more than just donating to a charity or handing someone a gift. It’s really about sharing what you have—your time, your money, maybe even just a little kindness. When you encourage a child to give, even in small ways, you’re teaching them empathy and gratitude. And you know what? They start to realize that their actions matter, that they can actually make a difference in someone’s life. That’s a pretty powerful lesson for any age.
Now, let’s talk saving. Saving is all about setting something aside for the future. It’s the quiet superpower behind dreams and security. When you save, you’re practicing patience, and you’re building up a sense of freedom—freedom to handle surprises, or to chase after big goals. If you make saving a habit, it doesn’t just grow your bank account; it eases your worries about what’s ahead. And honestly, who doesn’t want a little extra peace of mind?
Then comes spending. This is usually the part of money we notice the most—buying what we need, enjoying a treat now and then. But here’s the thing: if you only focus on spending, it’s easy to lose track and let money slip away on things that don’t really matter. That’s why it’s so important to spend with intention. Before you buy, ask yourself: Is this something I truly need? Will it bring lasting happiness? When you spend thoughtfully, you get to enjoy your money without looking back with regret.
These three pillars—giving, saving, and spending—they’re not meant to stand alone. If you forget one, everything can get a little wobbly. Imagine only saving and never giving—you might start to feel stingy. Or if you focus just on spending, you could end up in debt or feeling empty, no matter how much you buy.
So how do you make this real, especially for kids? Try this: picture three jars, each one labeled—Giving, Saving, and Spending. Whenever money comes in, whether it’s from an allowance, a birthday, or a little job around the house, split it up among those jars. It takes an idea that’s kind of abstract and makes it something you can see and touch. And it opens up conversations, too. How much should go in each jar? What’s the goal for each one?
The Giving Jar is for donations, gifts, or any act of kindness. The Saving Jar is all about future dreams or those moments when you need a safety net. And the Spending Jar? That’s for the everyday needs and those little joys that make life fun.
What’s great about this approach is how flexible it is. As kids grow, the jars can change with them. The real key is to be consistent. By making this a regular habit, managing money stops feeling overwhelming. It becomes second nature—something that helps you reach goals, help others, and enjoy what you’ve earned.
These three pillars also give families a common language when talking about money. Instead of just saying, “Be smart with your money,” you can sit down and chat about exactly how much to give, save, or spend. It makes the whole topic a lot clearer, and helps everyone stay on the same page.
So, here’s the key takeaway: giving, saving, and spending with purpose are the building blocks of true financial well-being. They offer a simple, memorable way to guide decisions—no matter how old you are. When you make these three pillars part of daily life, you’re laying the foundation for a future full of generosity, security, and really thoughtful choices.
